title: Frequency of Infraposition and Missing Contact Points in Implant-Supported Restorations within Natural Dentitions over Time: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis

subsections.section_title: Biological and Biomechanical Basis of Positional and Contact Changes Around Implant-Supported Restorations
subsections.subsection_title: Biological and Biomechanical Basis of Positional and Contact Changes Around Implant-Supported Restorations - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A fundamental premise for understanding infraposition and proximal contact loss is that osseointegrated implants behave biologically unlike natural teeth. Once integrated, an implant is essentially ankylosed to bone and lacks a periodontal ligament, so it does not participate in the adaptive eruption, axial drift, or cushioning mechanisms that characterize dentate occlusion. This biological stability is central to modern implant dentistry, but it also creates a positional mismatch over time when adjacent teeth continue to move within a remodeling craniofacial complex ref [3].

By contrast, natural teeth remain embedded in a viscoelastic periodontal apparatus that permits small but cumulative positional changes under function. Functional loading influences force transmission patterns in implant-supported prostheses differently from those in tooth-supported units, because implants have reduced micromobility and transfer forces more directly to the surrounding bone ref [14]. In a mixed dentition-implant environment, this difference means that physiologic eruption and mesial migration of neighboring teeth may continue while the implant restoration remains comparatively static, providing the biomechanical basis for apparent vertical discrepancy and the gradual opening of interproximal contacts.

These positional changes are expressed clinically through both hard- and soft-tissue interfaces. Peri-implant marginal bone configuration and restorative design features can affect the vertical and horizontal support of the peri-implant tissues ref [24], while papilla presence and embrasure fill depend strongly on the relationship among bone crest, contact area, and soft-tissue dimensions ref [25,29]. Accordingly, even minor relative tooth movement next to a stationary implant may translate into visible contact loss, altered papillary support, and food impaction risk, particularly when soft-tissue management and emergence profile control are suboptimal ref [33].

subsections.section_title: Biological and Biomechanical Basis of Positional and Contact Changes Around Implant-Supported Restorations
subsections.subsection_title: Biological and Biomechanical Basis of Positional and Contact Changes Around Implant-Supported Restorations - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A central biomechanical premise behind infraposition is that osseointegrated implants behave as ankylosed units, lacking the periodontal ligament-mediated adaptive mobility of natural teeth. As a result, implants are highly stable at the bone–implant interface, and their position is governed primarily by the mechanical and biological properties of peri-implant bone rather than by eruptive or orthodontic-like compensatory mechanisms seen in dentate teeth ref [10], ref [11]. This relative positional rigidity becomes clinically relevant when adjacent teeth continue to erupt, tip, or migrate over time.

The same implant immobility also helps explain loss of proximal contact points. Natural teeth exhibit small but continuous mesial drift, functional wear compensation, and positional adaptation under occlusal loading, whereas implant restorations remain comparatively fixed in space ref [27], ref [29]. Consequently, even minor long-term tooth movement can open interproximal contacts next to an implant crown. From a treatment-planning perspective, this distinction is particularly important in single-tooth replacement, where the implant restoration must coexist with neighboring teeth that retain lifelong adaptive capacity ref [24], ref [29].

These differences are not merely esthetic or prosthetic concerns; they reflect fundamentally different load-transfer systems. Whereas natural teeth distribute force through the periodontal ligament, implants transmit load directly to bone, producing a different biomechanical environment and a reduced capacity for positional accommodation ref [10], ref [11]. Therefore, infraposition and contact loss should be understood as expected consequences of the mismatch between a static ankylosis-like restoration and a dynamic natural dentition, rather than as isolated technical complications ref [27], ref [24].

subsections.section_title: Biological and Biomechanical Basis of Positional and Contact Changes Around Implant-Supported Restorations
subsections.subsection_title: Biological and Biomechanical Basis of Positional and Contact Changes Around Implant-Supported Restorations - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A central biomechanical explanation for infraposition is the disparity between the ankylosis-like fixation of osseointegrated implants and the lifelong positional adaptability of natural teeth. Because implants do not erupt with the adjacent dentition, even small continued eruption or vertical dentoalveolar development of neighboring teeth can make an implant-supported crown appear progressively apical over time. This phenomenon is particularly relevant in the anterior maxilla, where retrospective esthetic evaluations have shown that long-term harmony is sensitive to subtle vertical discrepancies between implant restorations and adjacent natural teeth ref [4].

The same biologic asymmetry also contributes to loss of proximal contact points. Natural teeth retain a periodontal ligament and therefore exhibit physiologic mesial drift, minor rotational change, and adaptive movement under occlusal loading, whereas the implant restoration remains comparatively stationary. Evidence from orthodontic biomechanics further illustrates the practical meaning of this difference: implants can serve as stable anchorage units precisely because they resist the displacement patterns seen in teeth subjected to orthodontic forces ref [24]. In mixed dentitions with implant-supported crowns, that difference in mobility and migration capacity can gradually open interproximal contacts despite initially accurate prosthetic design.

Peri-implant soft-tissue conditioning and provisionalization may improve the esthetic integration of implant crowns, but these measures mainly optimize contour and mucosal appearance rather than eliminate the underlying positional mismatch between a fixed implant and moving teeth ref [36]. Accordingly, biologic remodeling of the surrounding dentoalveolar complex and physiologic tooth migration should be regarded as ongoing drivers of both infraposition and contact loss, with prosthetic refinement serving primarily a compensatory, not preventive, role ref [4], ref [36].

subsections.section_title: Biological and Biomechanical Basis of Positional and Contact Changes Around Implant-Supported Restorations
subsections.subsection_title: Biological and Biomechanical Basis of Positional and Contact Changes Around Implant-Supported Restorations - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A further biomechanical contributor to apparent infraposition and proximal contact instability is the remodeling behavior of peri-implant crestal bone and the associated soft-tissue scaffold. Because implants are ankylosed, even small vertical or horizontal changes at the crestal complex can alter the relative position of the restoration margin and contact area compared with neighboring teeth that continue to erupt and migrate. Systematic evidence indicates that implant-abutment configuration influences marginal bone preservation, with platform switching generally associated with reduced crestal bone changes relative to platform matching designs, underscoring that peri-implant geometry can modulate the structural environment in which positional discrepancies become clinically evident ref [15]. Similar emphasis on crestal preservation is reflected in analyses of microthreaded implant designs, which seek to distribute stress and limit early marginal remodeling ref [11].

Surgical and site-related factors also shape the long-term stability of this peri-implant envelope. Comparisons of drilling protocols have shown that peri-implant bone loss may vary according to osteotomy preparation, suggesting that heat generation, compression, and early healing dynamics can influence the maintenance of crestal support ref [21]. Likewise, flap design affects peri-implant tissue healing, with flapless and flapped installation showing different soft- and hard-tissue responses during early maturation ref [12]. In horizontally or vertically deficient ridges, augmentation procedures such as ramus block grafting, lateral maxillary wall grafting, or sinus elevation with autogenous parietal bone are used to establish implant support, but these reconstructed sites remain dependent on graft integration and remodeling over time, which may affect the stability of the peri-implant crest and thereby the apparent relationship between implant restorations and adjacent dentition ref [16], ref [17], ref [19].

From a restorative perspective, the transmucosal profile further mediates how small skeletal or crestal changes translate into clinical contact loss. Techniques that customize the gingival emergence profile aim to support stable soft-tissue contours around implant crowns ref [22]. Although such measures do not prevent the continued eruption or mesial drift of natural teeth, they may reduce the extent to which minor peri-implant remodeling becomes expressed as open embrasures, food impaction, or visible vertical discrepancy. Thus, infraposition and loss of proximal contact should be understood not only as consequences of differential dentoalveolar movement, but also as outcomes amplified or attenuated by peri-implant bone preservation, surgical technique, and restorative contour management.

subsections.section_title: Biological and Biomechanical Basis of Positional and Contact Changes Around Implant-Supported Restorations
subsections.subsection_title: Biological and Biomechanical Basis of Positional and Contact Changes Around Implant-Supported Restorations - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
From a mechanistic standpoint, proximal contact loss and apparent infraposition are not determined solely by skeletal growth or physiologic tooth eruption; they are also modulated by restorative and peri-implant maintenance factors. Because the implant remains osseointegrated and positionally stable, any biologic or prosthetic condition that alters the contour of the crown, the peri-implant tissues, or the relative position of adjacent teeth can accentuate the discrepancy over time. Clinical reviews of implant restorations have emphasized that retention mode, access for maintenance, and prosthetic design influence complication patterns that may secondarily affect contact stability and food impaction risk ref [30].

Longer-term clinical studies likewise indicate that marginal tissue and bone behavior around implants evolves under function, even in otherwise successful restorations. Reports with 3- to 8-year follow-up have documented stable survival together with measurable radiographic and soft-tissue changes after loading, including in subcrestally placed and immediately loaded implants, suggesting that the peri-implant environment is dynamic rather than static ref [10], ref [15], ref [19], ref [21]. Although these studies were not designed specifically around contact-point loss, they support the broader biological premise that remodeling at the implant shoulder and restorative interface can modify embrasure form and perceived vertical relationships over time.

In addition, peri-implant inflammatory complications may indirectly worsen positional and contact discrepancies by producing soft-tissue swelling, recession, or crestal bone loss, each of which can alter papillary support and cervical crown morphology ref [35]. Thus, the emergence of infraposition-like discrepancies and missing proximal contacts should be viewed as a multifactorial phenomenon arising from the interaction of ankylosed implant behavior, continued movement of neighboring teeth, prosthetic design choices, and the long-term health of peri-implant tissues ref [30], ref [35].

subsections.section_title: Clinical Definitions, Diagnostic Criteria, and Outcome Measures
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Definitions, Diagnostic Criteria, and Outcome Measures - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A prerequisite for synthesizing evidence on implant infraposition and missing proximal contact points is a clear distinction between vertical positional change of the implant restoration and peri-implant soft-tissue change. Infraposition generally refers to an implant-supported crown appearing progressively more apical relative to adjacent natural teeth over time, whereas papilla loss or altered soft-tissue contour reflects changes in the gingival architecture rather than true vertical displacement of the restoration. Studies of single implants in the anterior maxilla have therefore emphasized separate clinical recording of crown level, papilla height, and radiographic tissue support to avoid conflating these outcomes ref [6], ref [29], ref [33].

For diagnostic purposes, soft-tissue based outcomes are commonly operationalized through papilla fill or papilla level at the mesial and distal aspects of single-implant crowns. Clinical and radiographic assessment of papilla level has been used to judge whether the interproximal embrasure is completely filled, partially filled, or open, thereby providing a clinically relevant proxy for the presence of a missing contact area or unaesthetic black triangle ref [6], ref [25]. This is particularly important because the appearance of an open interproximal space may arise from contact loss, papilla deficiency, or both; accordingly, outcome definitions should specify whether the endpoint is a mechanical loss of tooth-restoration contact, a soft-tissue deficiency, or a combined esthetic-functional complication ref [25], ref [33].

Across studies, outcome measures are further shaped by recognized biologic determinants of papilla stability, especially the vertical and horizontal dimensions of peri-implant soft tissue and the relationship between the contact point, crestal bone, and adjacent tooth support ref [25], ref [29]. For systematic review purposes, reports should therefore document: (1) how infraposition was identified clinically or radiographically; (2) how interproximal contact loss was tested; and (3) whether papilla-related indices were recorded as separate secondary outcomes. Such standardization improves comparability between studies and reduces misclassification when pooling data on long-term positional and interproximal changes around implant-supported restorations within natural dentitions ref [6], ref [29], ref [33].

subsections.section_title: Clinical Definitions, Diagnostic Criteria, and Outcome Measures
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Definitions, Diagnostic Criteria, and Outcome Measures - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A second methodological issue concerns how these outcomes are operationalized as measurable endpoints. Infraposition is most meaningfully defined as a vertical discrepancy between the implant-supported crown and adjacent natural teeth that develops over time, whereas a missing contact point denotes loss of proximal physical contact between the restoration and the neighboring dentition. Reviews on implant esthetics and prosthodontic planning emphasize that such endpoints should be distinguished from broader soft-tissue or cosmetic assessments, because they reflect specific positional and relational changes of the restoration within a dentition that continues to erupt, migrate, and remodel ref [27], ref [29].

From a diagnostic standpoint, studies have used heterogeneous approaches, ranging from direct clinical inspection with floss or shimstock-type contact testing to standardized photographs, stone casts, and radiographic or digital superimposition methods. Digital imaging has been highlighted as particularly relevant for longitudinal oral rehabilitation assessment because it can improve reproducibility of positional measurements, facilitate image registration across time points, and reduce reliance on subjective visual estimation alone ref [17]. This is especially important for small vertical changes, where the threshold separating a clinically negligible discrepancy from true infraposition may be narrow.

Outcome reporting should therefore specify the unit of analysis, the reference structure, and the temporal sequence of observations. Statistical and treatment-planning literature has noted that implant restorations and tooth-supported alternatives cannot be meaningfully compared unless sequencing, baseline conditions, and follow-up intervals are clearly defined ref [24]. In the context of single-tooth implants, prosthodontic reviews further suggest that contact stability and relative crown position should be treated as longitudinal outcomes rather than static success criteria, ideally reported as both prevalence and magnitude of change over time ref [29], ref [27].

subsections.section_title: Clinical Definitions, Diagnostic Criteria, and Outcome Measures
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Definitions, Diagnostic Criteria, and Outcome Measures - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A central methodological issue in this review is how the primary outcomes are operationalized. Infraposition is typically defined as a vertical discrepancy in which the implant-supported crown appears more apical relative to adjacent natural teeth over time, whereas a missing contact point denotes loss of proximal contact between the implant restoration and the neighboring dentition. Because these changes are often subtle and progressive, studies have relied on a combination of clinical inspection, standardized photographs, and radiographic assessment rather than a single uniform diagnostic test ref [14], ref [19].

Diagnostic criteria vary substantially across reports. Aesthetic outcome studies of single-tooth implants in the anterior maxilla have commonly inferred infraposition from comparative crown-edge or incisal-level relationships on follow-up photographs and casts, often as part of broader esthetic indices rather than as a standalone endpoint ref [14], ref [36]. In prospective implant trials, radiographic follow-up has been used primarily to document marginal tissue and bone stability, but these datasets can also support longitudinal interpretation of crown position when serial standardization is adequate ref [10]. Imaging guidance texts further emphasize that reproducible projection geometry and calibrated measurements are prerequisites if small vertical or interproximal changes are to be interpreted reliably ref [19].

For outcome reporting, the literature alternates between dichotomous outcomes (presence/absence of infraposition or open contact) and ordinal or continuous descriptors such as visible discrepancy, degree of esthetic impairment, or measurable vertical difference. This heterogeneity complicates pooling and likely contributes to between-study variability in estimated event frequency. For meta-analytic purposes, clearer reporting of threshold values, examiner calibration, and the exact modality used to detect contact loss or vertical discrepancy is essential ref [14], ref [10], ref [19], ref [36].

subsections.section_title: Clinical Definitions, Diagnostic Criteria, and Outcome Measures
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Definitions, Diagnostic Criteria, and Outcome Measures - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A further source of heterogeneity in outcome assessment is the distinction between biologic tissue change and prosthodontic positional change. Infraposition should not be inferred solely from marginal bone remodeling, because crestal adaptation around implants may occur without clinically visible vertical discrepancy of the crown relative to adjacent natural teeth. Systematic evidence on platform design and crestal bone behavior shows that peri-implant bone level change is commonly quantified radiographically at the implant shoulder–bone interface, an outcome that is related to but not equivalent to infraposition or proximal contact alteration ref [15], ref [11]. Accordingly, studies included in evidence synthesis should explicitly separate radiographic bone-level outcomes from clinically observed vertical step formation and from loss of interproximal contact.

Diagnostic criteria are also influenced by surgical and restorative context. In augmented sites or anatomically complex rehabilitations, baseline crown position and peri-implant reference landmarks may be altered by graft contour, implant angulation, or extensive prosthetic compensation, complicating longitudinal comparison ref [16], ref [19], ref [21], ref [9]. Similar interpretive caution applies in special-care cohorts restored with implant-supported fixed prostheses, where functional limitations may affect direct chairside assessment of contact integrity and occlusal relationships ref [33]. For meta-analytic purposes, outcome reporting is therefore strongest when studies specify the reference time point, the anatomic unit assessed (crown edge, contact area, or bone crest), and the method of detection used at follow-up.

From an operational standpoint, missing contact points are best treated as a dichotomous prosthodontic event at a defined proximal surface, whereas infraposition is better modeled as either a continuous vertical discrepancy or a threshold-defined categorical outcome. Broader implant success frameworks emphasize that diagnostic algorithms must prespecify loading conditions, radiographic controls, and functional endpoints ref [10]. This principle is directly relevant here: without predeclared thresholds and standardized measurement intervals, apparently similar studies may report fundamentally different outcome constructs, limiting pooled estimates and obscuring the true time-dependent frequency of infraposition and proximal contact loss.

subsections.section_title: Clinical Definitions, Diagnostic Criteria, and Outcome Measures
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Definitions, Diagnostic Criteria, and Outcome Measures - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A persistent source of heterogeneity in this literature is the way outcomes are recorded and reported. For infraposition, radiographic and photographic methods are often used interchangeably, yet they capture different dimensions of change: conventional radiography is most suitable for assessing hard-tissue landmarks and implant position, whereas standardized clinical photography and emerging digital imaging workflows are better suited to documenting vertical discrepancy at the crown level relative to adjacent natural teeth. Accordingly, outcome definitions should explicitly distinguish skeletal or implant positional stability from prosthetic infraocclusion as a visible clinical endpoint ref [23].

For missing contact points, the diagnostic unit should likewise be specified. Studies variably report contact loss as a binary prosthesis-level event, a site-specific mesial/distal event, or a patient-level prevalence measure, which impairs pooled synthesis. Because restoration design and retention mode can influence retrievability, maintenance, and the clinical verification of proximal contacts, reporting should also include prosthetic characteristics such as single crown versus fixed partial denture and cement-retained versus screw-retained design ref [30]. These descriptors do not define the outcome itself, but they are essential covariates for interpreting event frequency and follow-up findings ref [30].

From a meta-analytic perspective, a minimum reporting set should therefore include: the clinical definition used for infraposition and contact loss, the examination modality, the unit of analysis, threshold or scoring criteria, and the time point of assessment. Imaging protocols should be described sufficiently to judge reproducibility and measurement validity, especially when serial radiographs or digital methods are used to infer small positional changes over time ref [23]. Greater standardization in these outcome measures would substantially improve comparability across implant studies and reduce avoidable methodological noise in evidence synthesis ref [23, 30].

subsections.section_title: Epidemiology and Temporal Patterns of Infraposition and Contact Loss
subsections.subsection_title: Epidemiology and Temporal Patterns of Infraposition and Contact Loss - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
At the epidemiologic level, infraposition and proximal contact loss should be interpreted as time-dependent sequelae of the biologic discrepancy between osseointegrated implants and adjacent natural teeth. Because implants remain ankylosed while neighboring teeth continue to undergo eruption, migration, and periodontal adaptation, even initially satisfactory restorations may show progressive vertical and interproximal changes during follow-up. This conceptual framework is reflected in studies of peri-implant soft-tissue architecture, where papilla fill and crown–soft-tissue relationships are shown to depend strongly on the behavior of adjacent dentition rather than on the implant alone ref [6], ref [25], ref [29].

Although these references are not meta-analytic incidence studies per se, they consistently indicate that the frequency of visible discrepancy increases with observation time, particularly in single-tooth restorations bordered by natural teeth in esthetically demanding regions. Retrospective evaluation of papilla levels adjacent to anterior single implants demonstrated that small positional and tissue-level differences become clinically perceptible over time, supporting the cumulative nature of infraposition-related esthetic change ref [6]. Reviews on papilla management and peri-implant soft-tissue dimensions similarly emphasize that stable interproximal relationships are difficult to preserve long term when adjacent teeth continue physiologic movement, thereby predisposing to open contacts and papillary alterations ref [25], ref [29], ref [33].

Accordingly, the temporal pattern is best described as gradual rather than acute: early post-restorative harmony does not guarantee long-term positional stability. From a survey perspective, these studies provide the biologic and clinical basis for expecting increasing prevalence of both infraposition and missing contact points as follow-up extends, especially in younger patients and in the anterior maxilla where small vertical discrepancies are more readily detected ref [6], ref [25], ref [33].

subsections.section_title: Epidemiology and Temporal Patterns of Infraposition and Contact Loss
subsections.subsection_title: Epidemiology and Temporal Patterns of Infraposition and Contact Loss - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A consistent theme in the prosthodontic literature is that infraposition and loss of proximal contact around implant-supported single crowns should be understood as time-dependent events rather than static baseline defects. Because osseointegrated implants remain ankylosis-like relative to adjacent natural teeth, even small ongoing dentoalveolar changes can accumulate and become clinically perceptible during follow-up, particularly in esthetically sensitive regions ref [27], ref [29]. This framing is important epidemiologically, since cross-sectional prevalence estimates may underestimate the cumulative burden observed in longer observation periods.

The same temporal logic also helps explain why these complications are often discussed in treatment-sequencing papers comparing single implants with tooth-borne fixed partial dentures. In such decision models, the expected longevity of the restoration is not determined solely by implant survival, but also by whether adjacent teeth continue to erupt, migrate, or remodel over time, thereby increasing the probability of infraocclusion or open contacts as follow-up extends ref [24]. Accordingly, reports with longer maintenance intervals are more likely to identify progressive mismatch between the implant restoration and neighboring dentition, even when initial prosthetic and esthetic outcomes were satisfactory ref [24], ref [29].

From a survey perspective, these observations support interpreting frequency data as duration-sensitive outcomes. Apparent heterogeneity between studies may therefore reflect differences in patient age, esthetic zone involvement, and especially length of follow-up rather than contradictory biology. Reviews addressing functional and esthetic requirements for implants repeatedly emphasize long-term adaptation of the peri-implant-restorative complex, implying that infraposition and contact loss should be monitored longitudinally and reported cumulatively, not merely at delivery or short-term recall ref [27], ref [29].

subsections.section_title: Epidemiology and Temporal Patterns of Infraposition and Contact Loss
subsections.subsection_title: Epidemiology and Temporal Patterns of Infraposition and Contact Loss - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A consistent theme in longitudinal implant esthetic studies is that biologic and prosthetic discrepancies often become more evident with time rather than at delivery. In single-tooth implant restorations in the anterior maxilla, retrospective evaluation has shown that initially acceptable esthetic outcomes may later reveal relative vertical disharmony between the implant crown and adjacent natural teeth, a pattern compatible with progressive infraposition as the dentition continues to erupt or remodel while the implant remains ankylosed [4].

Short- to medium-term prospective data support this time-dependent interpretation. In a 3-year randomized clinical trial comparing submerged and transmucosal placement protocols, clinical and radiologic outcomes in the anterior maxilla and mandible were generally favorable, yet the study duration also illustrates that peri-implant tissue relationships and crown-tooth harmony must be monitored over repeated follow-up intervals rather than judged from baseline alone [10]. Similarly, randomized evidence on implant-supported crowns with and without peri-implant conditioning using provisional fixed prostheses indicates that soft-tissue and esthetic optimization at restoration delivery does not eliminate the possibility of later discrepancy relative to neighboring teeth [36].

Taken together, these studies suggest that the epidemiology of infraposition and proximal contact loss should be interpreted cumulatively: reported frequencies are likely to rise with longer observation because the underlying process is progressive and often subtle in early years [4], [10], [36]. This temporal behavior is particularly important in the anterior dentition, where even small vertical changes or loss of proximal adaptation may become clinically conspicuous during long-term maintenance [4], [36].

subsections.section_title: Epidemiology and Temporal Patterns of Infraposition and Contact Loss
subsections.subsection_title: Epidemiology and Temporal Patterns of Infraposition and Contact Loss - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A consistent theme across longitudinal implant literature is that biologic and prosthetic changes accumulate with time even when early integration is uneventful. Studies on immediate-loading decision algorithms and early peri-implant healing indicate that favorable primary stability and uncomplicated soft-tissue maturation mainly predict short-term osseointegration, but they do not eliminate later dimensional discrepancies between osseointegrated implants and adjacent natural teeth, which continue to erupt, migrate, and remodel over time [10, 12]. This distinction is important when interpreting infraposition and proximal contact loss as delayed complications rather than early treatment failures.

The time-dependent nature of these events is also supported indirectly by cohorts with demanding clinical circumstances and by protocols emphasizing rapid functional rehabilitation. Prospective treatment in patients with neurologic disabilities and immediate-function full-arch concepts such as the Maxillary V-4 approach demonstrate that restorations can remain serviceable during follow-up, yet they also underscore that complication profiles evolve as function continues and maintenance intervals lengthen [6, 9]. In partially dentate situations, this temporal framework helps explain why open contacts and relative implant crown infraocclusion are often low at delivery but become more prevalent during subsequent years of function.

Notably, procedural variables that are often associated with peri-implant tissue preservation—such as drilling approach, flap design, platform configuration, or customized emergence profile development—primarily address crestal bone behavior and peri-implant contour rather than the dentoalveolar changes of neighboring teeth [7, 8, 1]. Thus, while these factors may moderate local tissue stability, they are unlikely to fully prevent the cumulative epidemiologic rise in infraposition and missing contact points reported over time. The available evidence therefore supports a longitudinal interpretation in which risk increases with follow-up duration and should be incorporated into long-term recall planning and patient counseling.

subsections.section_title: Epidemiology and Temporal Patterns of Infraposition and Contact Loss
subsections.subsection_title: Epidemiology and Temporal Patterns of Infraposition and Contact Loss - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
Longer-term follow-up studies, although not always designed specifically to quantify infraposition or proximal contact loss, are informative for understanding their temporal behavior in implant-supported restorations within natural dentitions. Across observation windows of approximately 3 to 8 years, clinical reports consistently show that biologic and prosthetic outcomes remain broadly acceptable while minor positional and restorative discrepancies may accumulate over time, reinforcing the concept that these complications are predominantly progressive rather than early catastrophic events ref [10], ref [19], ref [21].

This time-dependent interpretation is particularly relevant for infraposition, because an osseointegrated implant remains ankylosed while adjacent natural teeth may continue eruption or exhibit dentoalveolar remodeling. Consequently, even restorations that appear satisfactory at delivery can display increasing vertical discrepancy at later recalls, especially in younger adults or in dentitions still undergoing subtle post-adolescent change. Medium- and long-term follow-up datasets therefore support the view that prevalence estimates should be interpreted cumulatively, with later examinations expected to detect more cases than short-term cross-sectional assessments ref [10], ref [21].

A similar cumulative pattern applies to missing proximal contacts. Clinical review evidence indicates that contact loss is influenced not only by time in function but also by prosthetic design and retention characteristics, which may affect maintenance needs and the stability of the restoration-tooth relationship ref [30]. Accordingly, 3-year and 6-year cohort data on fixed implant rehabilitations are best read as snapshots along an ongoing trajectory rather than final event rates, underscoring the need for repeated monitoring when estimating epidemiology over time ref [19], ref [21], ref [30].

subsections.section_title: Risk Factors and Sources of Heterogeneity
subsections.subsection_title: Risk Factors and Sources of Heterogeneity - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A major source of heterogeneity in reported infraposition and proximal contact loss is the peri-implant soft-tissue and crestal bone environment, because these variables directly affect the stability of papillae, crown contours, and interproximal relationships over time. Studies focused on papilla levels around single implants in the anterior maxilla indicate that soft-tissue fill is highly sensitive to local anatomical conditions and restorative design, making longitudinal comparisons across cohorts inherently variable ref [4]. This is reinforced by broader reviews on inter-dental/inter-implant papilla management and soft-tissue handling, which emphasize that tissue thickness, the distance to adjacent teeth, and the quality of peri-implant mucosal support are critical determinants of visible interproximal change ref [25], ref [33].

From a risk-factor perspective, reduced soft-tissue volume and unfavorable peri-implant dimensions may predispose restorations to apparent infraposition or to clinically detectable open contacts as neighboring dentition continues to erupt or drift while the implant remains ankylosed. Reviews on critical soft-tissue dimensions and treatment concepts suggest that inadequate horizontal or vertical tissue architecture can compromise papillary support and emergence profile stability, thereby amplifying the perception and severity of these complications ref [29]. Methodologically, this means that studies differing in baseline tissue phenotype, esthetic zone inclusion, and soft-tissue augmentation protocols are unlikely to yield directly comparable event rates ref [33], ref [25].

Crestal bone maintenance and load transfer further contribute to between-study variation. Meta-analytic evidence on platform switching indicates that restoration–implant interface design can influence marginal bone levels, which may secondarily affect the support of interproximal soft tissues and contact stability ref [24]. In parallel, biomechanical reviews note that functional forces alter stress distribution within implant-supported prostheses and surrounding bone, suggesting a plausible pathway by which occlusal loading differences may modulate long-term positional and contact changes ref [14]. Consequently, patient- and prosthesis-level differences in tissue phenotype, papilla-related anatomy, platform configuration, and functional loading should be treated as key moderators in any synthesis of infraposition and missing contact points ref [4], ref [24], ref [14].

subsections.section_title: Risk Factors and Sources of Heterogeneity
subsections.subsection_title: Risk Factors and Sources of Heterogeneity - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Implant- and prosthesis-related design variables are plausible contributors to heterogeneity in infraposition and loss of proximal contacts, even when direct causal evidence remains limited. Reviews on single-tooth implant prosthodontics emphasize that implant position, restorative contour, emergence profile, and occlusal scheme determine how the restoration interacts with adjacent natural teeth over time; these factors may modulate both perceived vertical discrepancy and the tendency for contact opening as the dentition continues to adapt while the implant remains ankylosed [27,29]. Statistical considerations in choosing a single implant versus a fixed partial denture further suggest that treatment selection itself may confound observed event rates because different prosthetic strategies distribute functional and positional changes differently within the arch [24].

Platform configuration is another likely source of between-study variation. Although platform switching has mainly been evaluated for marginal bone preservation rather than infraposition per se, meta-analytic data indicate that implant-abutment geometry can influence peri-implant hard-tissue behavior [16]. Because crestal bone support affects soft-tissue stability and restorative contour maintenance, studies mixing platform-switched and platform-matched implants may report different frequencies of open contacts or apparent infraposition. More broadly, esthetic and functional implant requirements include control of crown proportions, interproximal morphology, and load distribution, all of which can alter how subtle positional discrepancies are detected clinically [27].

Methodological heterogeneity also derives from variation in implant systems, loading protocols, and definitions of complications. Clinical risk-factor analyses of implant failure demonstrate that implant outcomes are sensitive to multiple interacting technical and patient variables, cautioning against simple extrapolation across cohorts [15]. In the present topic, comparable inconsistency likely arises when studies differ in follow-up duration, whether contact loss is scored clinically or radiographically, and whether infraposition is recorded as a continuous measurement or a dichotomous event. Prosthodontic reviews therefore support stratified interpretation by restoration design and clinical context rather than reliance on a single pooled estimate [24,29].

subsections.section_title: Risk Factors and Sources of Heterogeneity
subsections.subsection_title: Risk Factors and Sources of Heterogeneity - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
Implant- and restoration-related design choices are plausible contributors to heterogeneity in reported infraposition and proximal contact loss, even when they are not always isolated as primary study outcomes. In anterior single-tooth cohorts, aesthetic evaluations consistently indicate that the final vertical and mesiodistal relationship of the crown is sensitive to fixture position, transmucosal architecture, and crown contour, all of which may affect how stable the implant crown remains relative to adjacent natural teeth over time ref [4], ref [36]. These variables are particularly relevant in the maxillary anterior region, where even small discrepancies in vertical level or contact tightness become clinically perceptible.

Methodological differences in surgical protocol may further modify these outcomes. A randomized trial comparing submerged and transmucosal placement demonstrated that peri-implant tissue and radiologic behavior can differ according to placement approach, suggesting a pathway by which implant shoulder level, soft-tissue maturation, and restorative timing may indirectly influence the later expression of infraposition or loss of proximal contact ref [10]. Likewise, studies using provisionalization or peri-implant conditioning have shown that soft-tissue shaping and emergence profile control alter the esthetic integration of the definitive crown, which may also change how contact areas are positioned and maintained ref [36].

These factors are important sources of heterogeneity in meta-analysis because primary studies vary in implant system, placement depth, loading/restorative sequence, provisional crown use, and esthetic assessment methods. Retrospective aesthetic studies often combine different implant positions and prosthetic designs within the same sample, whereas randomized trials apply more standardized protocols but shorter follow-up windows ref [4], ref [10]. Consequently, pooled estimates for infraposition and missing contact points should be interpreted with caution, since part of the between-study variance likely reflects treatment-design diversity rather than only true biologic susceptibility.

subsections.section_title: Risk Factors and Sources of Heterogeneity
subsections.subsection_title: Risk Factors and Sources of Heterogeneity - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
Implant- and site-related design variables are plausible contributors to heterogeneity in infraposition and proximal contact loss, even when they are not direct causal determinants. Primary and secondary stability depend in part on implant diameter and localization, indicating that anterior versus posterior placement and local bone conditions may modify the long-term positional behavior of implant-supported restorations relative to adjacent teeth ref [13]. Likewise, immediate-loading diagnostic frameworks emphasize that bone quality, insertion torque, and local biomechanical conditions are interdependent variables, which can differ substantially across studies and thereby confound pooled estimates of longitudinal complications ref [10].

Marginal bone preservation around the implant neck may also influence the peri-implant soft-tissue architecture that supports stable interproximal relationships. Reviews of microthreaded implants suggest that collar design can affect crestal bone remodeling, while broader analyses of implant surface characteristics indicate that macro- and microtopography vary widely between systems and may influence tissue integration patterns ref [11], ref [31]. Experimental evidence further shows that inter-implant distance alters the peri-implant bone configuration, implying that spacing and platform-related design features should be considered when interpreting missing contact points or vertical discrepancies in multi-unit settings ref [21].

Host-site morphology introduces an additional source of variation. Baseline ridge defect configuration has been associated with differential implant outcomes in augmented posterior mandibles, underscoring that reconstructed sites may not behave like pristine ridges during long-term follow-up ref [25]. Soft-tissue conditions are similarly relevant: the presence or absence of keratinized mucosa has been linked to differences in peri-implant clinical outcomes, suggesting a potential pathway by which mucosal phenotype could affect contact stability and the apparent severity of infraposition over time ref [35]. Collectively, inconsistent reporting of these variables across studies remains a major source of methodological heterogeneity in meta-analytic synthesis.

subsections.section_title: Risk Factors and Sources of Heterogeneity
subsections.subsection_title: Risk Factors and Sources of Heterogeneity - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A major source of heterogeneity in reported rates of infraposition and proximal contact loss is methodological rather than purely biological. Studies differ substantially in how outcomes are detected and quantified, particularly with respect to radiographic modality, image standardization, and the distinction between vertical discrepancy, marginal bone remodeling, and apparent positional change caused by projection error. Reviews of implant imaging emphasize that conventional periapical radiographs, panoramic views, and cross-sectional techniques provide different levels of geometric reliability, which directly affects longitudinal comparability of small positional changes such as infraposition or subtle contact opening ref [23].

Clinical protocols may further confound pooled estimates because loading strategy, depth of placement, and surgical approach alter the peri-implant environment in ways that can influence bone remodeling and emergence profile. Immediate loading of subcrestally placed implants has been associated with specific hard- and soft-tissue responses that may modify the clinical visibility of vertical discrepancies over time ref [15]. Likewise, randomized comparison of immediate versus delayed loading in mandibular molar replacement and comparative assessment of flap versus flapless placement both show that treatment protocol can affect tissue stability and follow-up outcomes, even when implant survival remains high ref [21], ref [19]. These protocol-level differences should therefore be treated as potential effect modifiers in meta-analysis rather than as background noise.

Variation in implant stability assessment and prosthetic design also contributes to between-study inconsistency. Resonance frequency analysis has been proposed as an objective marker during early healing, but not all longitudinal studies report primary or secondary stability in a comparable way, limiting interpretation of whether later infraposition reflects growth-related tooth movement or early biomechanical conditions ref [34]. At the restorative level, cement- versus screw-retained reconstructions differ in retrievability, maintenance patterns, and complication profiles, which may influence the detection and management of missing contact points over time ref [30]. Finally, long-term clinical series of anodized-surface Brånemark implants illustrate how extended follow-up captures cumulative radiographic and prosthetic changes that shorter studies may miss, underscoring follow-up duration itself as a central source of heterogeneity ref [10].

subsections.section_title: Management Strategies and Preventive Clinical Implications
subsections.subsection_title: Management Strategies and Preventive Clinical Implications - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A primary preventive strategy for infraposition- and contact-related complications is prosthetically driven treatment planning that anticipates long-term soft-tissue and dentogingival change rather than only immediate osseointegration. In single-implant sites within natural dentitions, clinicians should assess smile line, periodontal phenotype, papilla support, and the spatial relationship to adjacent teeth before definitive restoration, because these variables influence the visible consequences of subsequent relative implant immobility and contact loss ref [5], ref [29], ref [33]. This is especially important in the anterior maxilla, where even limited vertical discrepancy or papillary deficiency may become clinically relevant over time ref [5].

From a management perspective, contouring of the transmucosal and cervical restorative complex should be regarded as a modifiable factor. Contemporary provisional fixed prosthodontic protocols support the use of interim restorations to sculpt emergence profile, guide peri-implant mucosal maturation, and test proximal form before the definitive crown is delivered ref [16], ref [33]. Such conditioning does not prevent skeletal or dental eruption changes, but it can optimize papilla fill and contact location at baseline, thereby improving resilience against future open contacts and esthetic deterioration ref [25], ref [29].

Preventive clinical implications therefore include delaying irreversible restorative decisions until soft-tissue architecture is stable, using provisionals to refine proximal contours, and documenting papilla level and contact relationships at insertion for later comparison. Where preoperative analysis suggests limited papillary support or thin soft tissue, clinicians should inform patients that maintenance, restorative modification, or eventual remake may be required as adjacent natural teeth continue to change over time ref [5], ref [25], ref [33].

subsections.section_title: Management Strategies and Preventive Clinical Implications
subsections.subsection_title: Management Strategies and Preventive Clinical Implications - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A central preventive strategy is to incorporate longitudinal risk assessment into treatment planning before implant placement. Because infraposition and proximal contact loss are time-dependent phenomena in dentitions that continue to remodel, the choice between a single-tooth implant and a tooth-borne fixed partial denture should be individualized rather than made on replacement alone. Statistical and sequencing considerations are particularly relevant in younger adults, in highly visible anterior sites, and in patients with ongoing occlusal or positional dental change, where the long-term maintenance burden of an implant restoration may be greater than initially anticipated ref [24].

At the prosthetic level, designs that facilitate retrievability, occlusal refinement, and periodic modification are preferable for patients at elevated risk. Reviews of single-tooth implant prosthodontics emphasize the importance of emergence profile control, contact-area morphology, and restorations that can be adjusted or remade if adjacent teeth migrate and contacts open over time ref [29]. Functional and esthetic planning should therefore anticipate future discrepancy rather than assuming static tooth-implant relationships, especially in the anterior region where even minor vertical disharmony becomes clinically evident ref [27].

Digital workflows strengthen prevention by enabling more precise baseline documentation and follow-up comparisons. Three-dimensional planning can improve implant positioning relative to anticipated prosthetic contours and adjacent teeth, while newer digital imaging and surface-registration approaches permit earlier recognition of vertical change, contour alteration, and interproximal discrepancies that may not be obvious on routine inspection ref [7], ref [17]. In parallel, soft-tissue management remains clinically important because favorable peri-implant tissue architecture may lessen the esthetic impact of small positional changes and simplify later corrective procedures, even if it does not eliminate the underlying risk of infraposition or contact loss ref [14].

subsections.section_title: Management Strategies and Preventive Clinical Implications
subsections.subsection_title: Management Strategies and Preventive Clinical Implications - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A central preventive strategy against later infraposition-related esthetic disharmony and loss of proximal contact is precise three-dimensional implant positioning at the outset of treatment. This requires prosthetically driven planning based on appropriate imaging, particularly cross-sectional assessment of alveolar form, neighboring roots, and buccolingual bone availability, so that the implant platform is not placed in a position that will magnify future discrepancies with adjacent natural teeth over time ref [19]. CT-based guide fabrication and contemporary surgical template concepts further improve transfer of the restorative plan to the operative field and help control mesiodistal spacing, depth, and angulation—variables directly relevant to emergence profile stability and contact-area design ref [8], ref [33].

Risk reduction should begin even earlier, during site development. In the esthetic zone, ridge/socket preservation may limit post-extraction collapse and maintain hard-tissue architecture needed for favorable implant placement relative to neighboring dentition ref [17]. When baseline soft-tissue volume is deficient, augmentation procedures can be used to improve peri-implant contour support and reduce the likelihood that small vertical discrepancies or open contacts become clinically conspicuous ref [32]. Such tissue-oriented planning is especially important in single-tooth sites where adjacent natural teeth may continue eruptive or compensatory movement while the implant remains ankylosed.

At the restorative stage, provisionalization can be used as a preventive tool rather than merely a cosmetic step. Peri-implant conditioning with provisional fixed prostheses supports the development of a more harmonious soft-tissue profile and may facilitate more controlled shaping of the interproximal region before definitive crown delivery ref [36]. Long-term retrospective esthetic data for single implants in the anterior maxilla further emphasize that implant position and peri-implant tissue management are major determinants of stable appearance, underscoring the need for integrated surgical-prosthetic planning from diagnosis through final restoration ref [32].

subsections.section_title: Management Strategies and Preventive Clinical Implications
subsections.subsection_title: Management Strategies and Preventive Clinical Implications - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A practical preventive strategy for limiting the clinical consequences of infraposition and loss of proximal contacts is meticulous peri-implant soft-tissue conditioning at the restorative stage. Customized emergence profiles can be used to support a more stable transmucosal architecture, improve crown contour transfer, and facilitate cleansability, all of which are relevant when long-term remodeling may expose esthetic discrepancies or food-impaction sites adjacent to natural teeth ref [8]. In this context, provisionalization and individualized contour development should be viewed not only as esthetic procedures but also as risk-mitigation measures within long-term maintenance.

Soft-tissue phenotype management is equally important. The presence of keratinized mucosa has been associated with more favorable clinical handling and may contribute to improved peri-implant tissue tolerance and hygiene access; conversely, limited keratinized tissue can complicate plaque control and maintenance around implant restorations, particularly when open contacts develop over time ref [35]. When the peri-implant mucosal conditions are suboptimal, clinicians should consider modifying the surgical or prosthetic approach early, rather than waiting for recurrent inflammation or patient-reported food packing to necessitate corrective treatment ref [35].

Accordingly, preventive care should integrate restorative contour control, assessment of keratinized tissue width, and individualized recall protocols. Patients at elevated risk of continuing dentoalveolar change or soft-tissue instability should be monitored for early contact loss, papilla flattening, and hygiene difficulty, with timely polishing, contour adjustment, remake of the proximal surface, or soft-tissue intervention as indicated ref [8], ref [35]. Such measures do not eliminate biologic change, but they can reduce the functional and esthetic burden of these common long-term complications.

subsections.section_title: Management Strategies and Preventive Clinical Implications
subsections.subsection_title: Management Strategies and Preventive Clinical Implications - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A practical endpoint of managing infraposition and proximal contact loss is the establishment of a structured maintenance pathway that links prosthetic review, soft-tissue assessment, and interdisciplinary retreatment planning. In adults requiring implant therapy in orthodontically or esthetically sensitive sites, treatment sequencing should anticipate continued dentoalveolar change and possible discrepancy between ankylosed implants and adjacent natural teeth; this makes long-term surveillance an integral part of care rather than a post hoc response to complications ref [11], ref [14]. Follow-up should therefore document vertical relationships, papilla fill, hygiene access, and patient-reported food impaction or esthetic dissatisfaction, since these findings often precede more overt biologic or prosthetic complications.

When intervention is needed, management should be tailored to the dominant problem. Minor open contacts or papillary deficiency may be approached prosthetically by modifying contour and emergence to support soft-tissue re-adaptation, including additive composite-based tissue modeling during provisional or definitive refinement ref [25]. Retention design also has preventive implications: screw-retained restorations generally facilitate retrievability and repeated adjustment when contacts open or vertical discrepancies become more evident, whereas cement-retained designs require greater caution because excess cement may complicate maintenance and inflammation control ref [30]. Because proximal contact loss can promote plaque accumulation and food impaction, timely correction is also relevant to prevention of peri-implant disease ref [35].

Imaging should be used selectively to support, rather than replace, clinical examination. Conventional radiography and cross-sectional imaging are valuable when evaluating crestal support, implant position relative to adjacent teeth, or the feasibility of prosthetic revision, particularly in complex esthetic zones ref [23]. Overall, the preventive message is that implants placed within natural dentitions require lifelong review, with early identification of occlusal, periodontal, and esthetic changes enabling conservative correction before infraposition or contact loss progresses to biologic or patient-centered failure ref [14], ref [35].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Framework for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
subsections.subsection_title: Methodological Framework for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
This review should be structured as a systematic synthesis of longitudinal evidence on implant infraposition and proximal contact loss in implant-supported restorations placed within natural dentitions. At the protocol stage, the review question must define the population, restoration type, comparator framework where applicable, follow-up horizon, and outcome metrics, while prespecifying how repeated observations over time will be handled. Methodological rigor is strengthened by adopting established systematic-review principles commonly used in implant dentistry, particularly those seen in Cochrane-style assessments of surgical and prosthetic interventions, where explicit eligibility criteria, duplicate study selection, and transparent risk-of-bias appraisal are central design features ref [15], ref [18], ref [19].

Eligibility criteria should prioritize human clinical studies reporting measurable infraposition, open or lost interproximal contacts, or both, after functional loading of implant-supported single crowns or fixed restorations adjacent to natural teeth. Because outcome frequency is likely influenced by treatment context, data extraction should also capture variables that may later explain heterogeneity, including augmentation history, implant site characteristics, restoration design, and digitally guided versus conventional placement workflows ref [21]. Related meta-analytic work in implant dentistry shows that surgically and prosthetically heterogeneous studies can still be pooled meaningfully when subgroup structure and outcome definitions are specified a priori ref [21], ref [24].

A final methodological principle for this review is to distinguish clearly between frequency, incidence over time, and longitudinal change. This is especially important because infraposition and contact loss are progressive phenomena rather than single end points. Accordingly, the review framework should anticipate separate syntheses for baseline-to-follow-up change and for time-specific prevalence estimates, with careful interpretation of pooled estimates in light of differences in peri-implant bone behavior, adjunctive augmentation procedures, and technical protocols documented across implant systematic reviews ref [15], ref [18], ref [19], ref [24].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Framework for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
subsections.subsection_title: Methodological Framework for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A central methodological requirement in this review is the prespecification of clinically meaningful effect modifiers before quantitative pooling. For outcomes such as infraposition frequency and loss of proximal contact over time, heterogeneity is expected to arise from differences in implant positioning concepts, implant–abutment configuration, surgical approach, restorative design, and comparator choice. Prior meta-analyses in implant dentistry illustrate how treatment effects can vary according to placement angulation, platform-switching strategies, and flapless versus flapped surgery, supporting an a priori subgroup framework rather than post hoc data partitioning ref [11], ref [16], ref [23].

Accordingly, data extraction should capture variables that may influence both event occurrence and observed frequency: implant location, patient age and growth status, duration of follow-up, radiographic or digital measurement method, prosthesis type, contact definition, and occlusal/prosthodontic design features. Reviews of digital imaging methods emphasize that measurement modality can materially affect the detection threshold for subtle vertical discrepancies, which is particularly relevant for infraposition assessments over long observation periods ref [17]. Likewise, prosthodontic reviews on single-tooth implants indicate that crown contour, interproximal morphology, and restorative sequencing may modify contact stability and therefore should be considered in stratified analyses or meta-regression when sufficient studies are available ref [24], ref [29].

Interpretation of pooled estimates should therefore prioritize consistency across these predefined domains rather than relying solely on a single summary proportion. Where subgroup patterns remain unstable because of sparse data, a structured narrative synthesis is preferable, with quantitative findings presented as conditional on methodological and clinical diversity rather than as universally transportable estimates ref [11], ref [23], ref [17].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Framework for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
subsections.subsection_title: Methodological Framework for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
For quantitative synthesis, the review should treat infraposition and missing contact points as time-dependent outcomes and pool them as proportions or cumulative event frequencies at prespecified follow-up intervals. Given the expected variability in restoration design, jaw location, age profile, and observation period, a random-effects framework is methodologically preferable to a fixed-effect approach. This choice is consistent with broader implant-related systematic reviews in which substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity is anticipated across studies and pooled estimates are therefore interpreted as average effects across diverse settings rather than a single common parameter ref [6], ref [7], ref [16].

Heterogeneity assessment should extend beyond a global inconsistency statistic and include subgrouping by follow-up duration, anterior versus posterior sites, and single-unit versus multi-unit prosthetic contexts wherever reported. Sensitivity analyses are particularly important because retrospective cohorts, nonstandardized radiographic methods, and inconsistent definitions of contact loss can materially shift pooled frequencies. Experience from augmentation meta-analyses shows that long-term outcomes are strongly influenced by baseline defect severity, surgical protocol, and reporting quality; by analogy, these factors justify cautious stratification and conservative interpretation in implant-restoration epidemiology ref [6], ref [7].

Interpretation of pooled findings should therefore emphasize not only the summary estimate but also the confidence interval width, between-study dispersion, and the clinical plausibility of temporal trends. In evidence domains characterized by long follow-up and heterogeneous treatment pathways, meta-analysis is most informative when used to map the likely range of event frequencies rather than to imply precise universal rates. This principle, evident in implant augmentation reviews and randomized meta-analytic comparisons, is directly applicable when synthesizing infraposition and proximal contact instability over time within natural dentitions ref [7], ref [16].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Framework for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
subsections.subsection_title: Methodological Framework for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A critical component of the meta-analytic framework is the explicit handling of clinical and methodological heterogeneity before pooling frequency estimates for infraposition and proximal contact loss. Although the target outcomes are prosthetic rather than purely peri-implant biologic, variations in implant design, crestal bone behavior, and surgical approach can plausibly modify long-term positional stability and interproximal relationships. Systematic reviews on platform switching and microthreaded implants illustrate how seemingly modest design differences may alter marginal bone remodeling, thereby creating indirect sources of between-study heterogeneity that should be explored in subgroup or sensitivity analyses rather than ignored in a single pooled model ref [15], ref [11].

Accordingly, prespecified effect modifiers should include implant-abutment configuration, macrodesign features, flap versus flapless surgery, and the use of adjunctive augmentation procedures. Reviews of flapless surgery and growth-factor-assisted bone augmentation show that surgical protocols differ substantially in tissue handling, healing dynamics, and peri-implant hard-tissue response, all of which may influence the long-term emergence profile and contact stability of implant-supported crowns within natural dentitions ref [26], ref [23]. Even when these variables are not the primary focus of individual studies, they should be extracted systematically because they may explain dispersion in reported frequencies over time.

For interpretation, pooled estimates should therefore be presented alongside heterogeneity statistics and a narrative assessment of biologic plausibility. If substantial inconsistency is detected, random-effects synthesis should be retained, but emphasis should shift toward identifying moderators and assessing robustness after excluding studies with markedly different surgical or implant-design characteristics. This approach, widely used in implant-related systematic reviews and meta-analyses, strengthens inference by distinguishing a true time-related increase in infraposition or contact loss from variability attributable to treatment protocol differences ref [15], ref [11], ref [26].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Framework for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
subsections.subsection_title: Methodological Framework for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
Interpretation of pooled estimates for infraposition and proximal contact loss should explicitly account for clinical heterogeneity that may not be fully captured by statistical models. In this literature, variation in pre-implant site development, including ridge preservation and more extensive vertical augmentation procedures, can alter baseline hard- and soft-tissue architecture and thereby influence the apparent longitudinal frequency of positional or contact changes around implant-supported crowns within natural dentitions [9, 24]. Consequently, meta-analytic conclusions should be framed as average effects across diverse treatment pathways rather than universal incidence values.

Sensitivity analyses are also essential when studies differ in surgical execution, loading protocol, imaging modality, and prosthetic design. Differences between flap and flapless placement, immediate versus delayed loading, and restoration retention concepts may modify peri-implant tissue behavior, occlusal settling, maintenance access, and measurement reproducibility, all of which can affect observed rates of infraposition or missing contact points over time [19, 21, 30]. Likewise, radiographic and cross-sectional imaging approaches differ in precision and dimensional information, so outcome ascertainment methods should be considered when assessing between-study inconsistency and risk of detection bias [23].

From a review-methods perspective, final evidence grading should therefore integrate not only pooled frequency estimates, but also confidence intervals, residual heterogeneity, methodological limitations, and indirectness arising from mixed clinical scenarios. Where subgroup data are sparse, narrative synthesis remains necessary to explain why similar nominal follow-up durations may yield different event frequencies across studies with distinct augmentation histories, operative protocols, and prosthetic configurations [9, 23, 24]. This interpretive framework strengthens the clinical applicability of the meta-analysis while avoiding overgeneralization.
